knownFor.label: Muslin & chintz
knownFor.note: Fine Bengal muslin and printed chintz.

location.value: Northern and central South Asia. At its peak under Aurangzeb it stretched from the Indus basin and Afghanistan to Assam and Bangladesh, and south into the Deccan plateau.

terrain.value: The fertile Indo-Gangetic plain, the Deccan plateau, and mountain frontiers to the northwest. Capitals at Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore and Delhi.

climate.value: Monsoon-dependent. Failed monsoons caused severe famines, e.g. the Deccan famine of 1630–32.

resources.value: Rich farmland (rice, wheat, cotton, indigo, sugar), Bengal textiles and silk, and diamonds from Golconda after its conquest.

disasters.value: Famines linked to monsoon failure (1630–32 Deccan famine).

population.value: About 150 million around 1600 and 158 million around 1700 (Wikipedia infobox), one of the largest populations in the world.

urbanisation.value: Large cities such as Agra, Delhi (Shahjahanabad), Lahore and Dhaka, each with hundreds of thousands of people.

disease.value: Epidemics followed famines. Specific outbreaks are not detailed in the sources checked.

migration.value: Persian, Central Asian and Afghan nobles, soldiers and scholars came to serve the court.

economicBase.value: Agricultural taxes, introduced systematically by Akbar, were the basis of the empire’s wealth. They took well over half a peasant’s output and were paid in silver.

tradeRoutes.value: Textiles (especially Bengal cottons) and spices exported via Indian Ocean ports (Surat, Hooghly). European companies (Portuguese, Dutch, English, French) bought Indian goods with American silver.

wealth.value: One of the world’s largest economies, though GDP estimates vary. Relative peace in the 17th century helped India’s economic expansion.

moneyAndTax.value: A standardised silver rupee, with copper dam coins. Land revenue assessed under Akbar’s system (Todar Mal’s reforms).

inequality.value: Very high: a small mansabdar (ranked noble) elite and the emperor took a large share of output from peasants and artisans.

governmentType.value: A monarchy under an emperor (padishah), with nobles ranked by the mansabdari system and provinces (subahs) run by governors.

keyRulers.value: Babur (1526–1530, founder). Humayun. Akbar (1556–1605). Jahangir. Shah Jahan (1628–1658). Aurangzeb (1658–1707, greatest extent). Bahadur Shah II (1837–1857, last).

succession.value: No fixed rule: princes fought wars of succession. For example, Aurangzeb defeated and executed his brother Dara Shikoh to take the throne.

institutions.value: Akbar’s centralised, standardised administration (mansabdari ranks, land revenue system, provinces). Persian as the language of government. The Fatawa ʿAlamgiri law compilation under Aurangzeb.

stability.value: An interruption under Sher Shah Suri (1540–1555). Revolts by Marathas, Sikhs, Jats and others in the late 17th–18th centuries.

eliteConflict.value: Succession wars between princes, and rivalry between noble factions (Iranis, Turanis, Afghans, Rajputs) after 1707.

armyAndTech.value: One of the “gunpowder empires” (with the Ottomans and Safavids). Babur used field artillery and firearms at Panipat (1526). Large cavalry armies supplied by the mansabdars.

majorWars.value: The First Battle of Panipat (1526) and Second (1556). Deccan wars against the Marathas (1680–1707). Nader Shah’s invasion and sack of Delhi (1739).

territoryChange.value: About 3.2 million km² around 1600 and 4.0 million km² in 1690 (Wikipedia infobox). Reduced to the area around Delhi by 1760.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Afghans (Sur), Rajput kingdoms (many later allied by marriage), the Deccan sultanates, the Marathas, the Safavids (over Kandahar), and later the British East India Company.

inventions.value: Advanced metalwork (astrolabes, seamless celestial globes), Damascus-steel weapons, and rocket artillery in the later period.

scienceEducation.value: Persian and Islamic scholarship, observatories, and translations of Sanskrit texts into Persian under Akbar.

openness.value: Akbar held interfaith debates and founded the syncretic Din-i Ilahi (1582). The court welcomed European travellers and Jesuits, though less so under Aurangzeb.

communicationTransport.value: The Grand Trunk Road with sarais (inns); ports such as Surat; runners and horse posts.

religion.value: Islam was the state religion; Hinduism was the majority religion, and Sikhism and others were present. Akbar was notably tolerant (abolishing the jizya tax on non-Muslims, 1564); Aurangzeb reimposed it (1679).
religion.source: Wikipedia: Mughal Empire (checked 5 Nov 2026) (infobox); Richards, The Mughal Empire (1993)

languageWriting.value: Persian was the official language. Hindustani (the ancestor of Hindi and Urdu) developed from the mix of Persian and local languages.

artsArchitecture.value: The Taj Mahal (Shah Jahan), the Red Fort, Humayun’s Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri and Lahore Fort, plus Mughal miniature painting.

socialStructure.value: Emperor and mansabdar nobility (Muslim and Hindu Rajput), zamindar landholders, merchants and artisans, and peasants. The Hindu caste system continued.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the dynasty and a shared Indo-Persian court culture. The name “Mughal” comes from “Mongol”, though the founders were Chagatai Turks.

dailyLife.value: Mud and brick houses for most people; bread, rice, lentils and spiced dishes; gardens and palaces for the elite.

neighbours.value: Safavid Persia, the Uzbeks, the Deccan sultanates, the Marathas, Rajput states, and the Portuguese, Dutch, English and French trading companies.

ideasReligions.value: A blend of Persian, Islamic and Indian traditions in art, music, food and language.

colonisation.value: As conqueror, it absorbed most of South Asia. As colonised, it was gradually taken over by the British East India Company from the mid-18th century, beginning with Bengal.

riseSignals.value: Babur’s victory at Panipat (1526) with firearms and artillery. Akbar’s efficient, centralised administration and policy of including Hindu Rajput elites.

peakPeriod.value: Court splendour peaked under Shah Jahan. The greatest extent came under Aurangzeb, around 1690.

declineSignals.value: Costly Deccan wars, succession disputes and weak rulers after 1707, regional powers breaking away, Nader Shah’s sack of Delhi (1739), and the rise of the East India Company. Historians disagree about Aurangzeb’s role.

outcome.value: Reduced to the area around Delhi. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the British exiled the last emperor, Bahadur Shah II, to Burma (1858) and formally dissolved the empire.

sources.value: Persian chronicles (Akbarnama, Ain-i-Akbari), revenue records, European travellers’ accounts and monuments. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Richards (1993).

overallCertainty.value: Good for politics. The end date depends on definition (1707, 1720 or 1857), and the start is sometimes dated to 1600 for its imperial structure. Population and GDP are estimates.
